title: Review: Active transport, bulk transport and co-transport; Nucleotides, DNA and RNA structure; Transcription
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM10a#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE04b#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE04b#t1 term and clue written for the game; GE04a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM10a#N.2a, GE04a#N.5, GE04b#N.8, MB04#N.3a, BM10a#N.12a, GE04a#N.11, GE04b#N.10a, BM10a#N.9, GE04a#N.3a, BM10a#N.11a, BM10a#N.8. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Double helix
items.clue: Shape formed when two base-paired polynucleotide strands twist together

items.label: Introns
items.clue: Sections removed from the transcript; 980 of 1608 bases in the human β-globin example.

items.label: Pre-mRNA
items.clue: First product when a whole eukaryotic gene is transcribed, before any sections are removed.

items.label: RNA polymerase
items.clue: Enzyme that binds at the start of a gene and joins adjacent nucleotides of the new transcript.

questions.stem: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?

options.text: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.

questions.explanation: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.

questions.stem: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.

questions.stem: Using the β-globin gene data, what percentage of the pre-mRNA is kept in the mature mRNA?

Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?

options.text: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.

questions.stem: A solution of DNA is heated to 95 °C. The two strands separate, but each strand remains a continuous, intact chain of nucleotides. Which explanation is consistent with these observations?

options.text: The backbone of each strand is covalently bonded, so it survives heating that breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds between the strands.
The hydrogen bonds of the backbone are stronger than the covalent bonds between strands, so only the strands come apart.
Heating breaks the covalent bonds that join the two strands, while the hydrogen bonds within each strand stay intact.
The bases along each strand are covalently bonded to one another, which holds the strand together when the pairs separate.

questions.stem: α-Amanitin, a toxin from the death cap mushroom, blocks the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in eukaryotic cells. It has no effect on DNA polymerase or on ribosomes. Which prediction about liver cells exposed to it is correct?

options.text: DNA replication stops, because the cells can no longer separate their DNA strands.
Translation of mRNA already in the cytoplasm stops at once.
No new mRNA is made, so protein synthesis falls as the existing mRNA is broken down.
The DNA of the cells' genes is damaged, so their base sequences change.

questions.explanation: Without RNA polymerase there is no transcription and no new mRNA. Proteins are made only until the existing mRNA runs out.

questions.stem: The human genome contains about 20 000 protein-coding genes, yet human cells produce well over 20 000 different polypeptides. Which process accounts for this?

options.text: Alternative splicing, in which different combinations of exons from one pre-mRNA are joined to give different mature mRNAs.
Mutation of the gene during transcription, so that each transcript carries a slightly different base sequence.
Degeneracy of the genetic code, which allows a codon to be translated as different amino acids in different cells.
Duplication of each gene during differentiation, so that every different polypeptide is coded for by a separate gene of its own.

questions.stem: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA from a hypothetical bacterium shows that 21% of its nitrogenous bases are adenine. What percentage of its bases are cytosine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so T = A = 21% and A + T = 42%. That leaves 100% − 42% = 58% for C and G together, and because C = G, cytosine is 58%/2 = 29%.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?

options.text: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA

questions.explanation: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, giving AUGCGUA.

questions.stem: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?

options.text: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.

questions.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how the two strands of a DNA double helix are held together?

options.text: By hydrogen bonds between identical bases, such as A with A, one on each strand
By covalent bonds between complementary bases, with one base on each strand
By hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one base on each strand
By covalent bonds joining the sugar–phosphate backbones of the two strands

questions.explanation: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one from each strand: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. The nucleotides within each strand are joined by covalent bonds.
